beats.intro: Chapter twenty-five. [[sub]]Agreement across the wire: split the data, commit as one.
beats.ground: One giant shop table, customers everywhere. [[cut]]Cut it: northern rows live north, salary columns live with payroll. Each piece lives near its users: less chatter, faster local answers. [[w]]Write this: fragments live near users to cut communication cost.
beats.frag: Two ways to cut. [[horiz]]Horizontal: split rows by predicate. North rows here, south rows there. Rebuild with union. [[vert]]Vertical: split columns, and repeat the primary key in every piece. Rebuild by joining on that key. [[props]]Good fragments are complete, reconstructible, and disjoint. [[w]]Write this: rows-union, columns-join-on-key, key repeated.
beats.q1: Quick check. [[q]]A vertically fragmented table is rebuilt with what?
beats.twopc: Now commit across sites as one. [[ask]]The coordinator asks every participant: prepare? Each records a prepared state. [[vote]]Each votes yes or no. [[decide]]All yes means commit; any no means abort. Everyone records and executes the decision. Atomicity holds globally: no lone commits, no lone aborts. [[w]]Write this: ask, vote, decide; no lone outcomes.
beats.q2: Quick check. [[q]]In two-phase commit, one participant votes no. Result?
beats.block: The price of agreement. [[stuck]]A prepared participant that cannot learn the decision waits. And waits. That waiting is called blocking. [[trap]]And a warning: two-phase commit is a commit protocol, never a locking protocol. [[w]]Write this: prepared plus silence equals blocking; commit, not locking.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Rows split by predicate, rebuilt by union; columns split with the key repeated, rebuilt by join. [[w2]]Ask, vote, decide: atomicity across every site. [[w3]]Blocking is the price; and it is a commit protocol, not locking.
